column2: Shunahshepha, it is said, became Vishvamitra's son; he had been assigned to be the sacrificial victim at Harishchandra's sacrifice.
Given by the gods, Shunahshepha was again given to Vishvamitra; because he was given by the gods, he became Devarata.
Devarata and the others, seven in all, were Vishvamitra's sons; Drishadvati's son too, and Vaishvamitra and Ashtaka.
Ashtaka's son Lauhi has been named; the Jahnu group has been told by me. Hereafter I shall tell the lineage of the great-souled Ayu.
He slew all the Danavas who were unslayable even by the thunderbolt-wielder; the lord regained the supreme fortune of the gods that had been lost.
Having killed all the Danavas, the lord Raji took it back. Then Indra with the gods said to the mighty Raji:
I am Raji's son, he said, and again spoke: "You are Indra of all the gods, father, no doubt here.
Whose son I am, Indra — by my deeds I shall gain fame." Hearing Indra's words, he was deceived by that illusion;
the king, pleased, said to Shatakratu, "So be it." When that king had gone to heaven, equal to the gods,
Raji's sons took the inheritance, the kingdom, from Indra; his five hundred sons took that very position of Shatakratu.
They overran in many ways the heavenly world, Trivishtapa. When they became deluded in themselves, maddened by passion, unrighteous,
haters of Brahmins, with their strength and valour destroyed, then Indra regained his lordship and his supreme station,
having slain all of Raji's sons, intent on lust and anger. One who hears or holds this account of Indra's fall from and re-establishment in his position will not meet with misfortune.
Rambha was childless; I shall now tell the lineage of Anenas. Anenas's son was the king Pratikshatra of great fame.
Pratikshatra's son was the renowned Sanjaya; Sanjaya's son was Jaya, and his son Vijaya.
Vijaya's son was Kriti; his son Haryavata; Haryavata's son was the mighty king Sahadeva.
Sahadeva's son, righteous-souled, was Nadina; Nadina's was Jayatsena; Jayatsena's was Sankriti.
Sankriti's son was the righteous, greatly famed Kshatravriddha; of Anenas's line another of Kshatravriddha is also named.
Kshatravriddha's son there was the greatly famed Sunahotra; Sunahotra had three heirs, exceedingly righteous:
Kasha, Shala, and the lord Gritsamada. Gritsamada's son was Shunaka, whose son was Shaunaka;
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and likewise Shudras (came from this line). Shala's son was Arshtisena, whose son was Kashyapa.
Kasha's son was the king Kashipa, and Dirghatapas; Dirghatapas's son Dhanus; then the learned Dhanvantari.
At the end of great austerity, the wise old man (obtained) Dhanvantari again, the god, born among humans in this life.
In his house the god Dhanvantari then arose as the Kashi king, the great king, destroyer of all diseases.
Having obtained Ayurveda from Bharadvaja here, he, devoted to physician's work, divided it again into eight parts and imparted it to disciples.
Dhanvantari's son was renowned as Ketuman; then Ketuman's son is remembered as the hero Bhimaratha.
Bhimaratha's son was the lord of creatures Divodasa; the righteous-souled Divodasa became ruler of Varanasi.
At that very time, Brahmins, a Rakshasa named Kshemaka settled the deserted city of Varanasi.
For it had been cursed by the wise, great-souled Nikumbha: "It shall be empty for a thousand years, no doubt."
As soon as it was cursed, the lord of creatures Divodasa established a lovely city on the Gomati at the edge of his country.
Varanasi had formerly been the city of Bhadrashrenya. Bhadrashrenya's hundred sons, excellent archers,
King Divodasa killed and settled there; by that stronger one Bhadrashrenya's kingdom was seized.
Bhadrashrenya's son, famed as Durdama, was released by Divodasa out of pity, thinking "he is a child."
The king took back the Haihaya inheritance, the paternal inheritance that Divodasa had seized by force.
By Bhadrashrenya's son, the great-souled Durdama, the end of the enmity was brought about, fortunate ones, through his own prowess.
From Divodasa, on Drishadvati, the hero Pratardana was born; by that child son the force was struck back.
Pratardana had two famed sons, Vatsa and Bharga; Vatsa's son was Alarka, and Alarka's son Sannati.
Alarka was a son, devoted to Brahmins, true to his word. About the royal sage Alarka a verse was sung by the ancients:

For sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years, young and endowed with beauty, the upholder of the family lived,
brahmapuran:11:53	by the grace of Lopamudra attaining a supreme lifespan; he had a very great kingdom, possessed of beauty and youth.
At the end of the curse, the mighty-armed one, having killed the Rakshasa Kshemaka, settled the lovely city of Varanasi again.
Sannati's heir was the righteous Sunitha; Sunitha's heir was the greatly famed Kshema.
Kshema's son was Ketuman, whose son was Suketu; Suketu's son is remembered as Dharmaketu.
Dharmaketu's heir was the great charioteer Satyaketu; Satyaketu's son was the lord of creatures named Vibhu.
Anarta was Vibhu's son and his son Sukumara; Sukumara's son was the very righteous Dhrishtaketu.
Dhrishtaketu's heir was the lord of creatures Venuhotra; Venuhotra's son was the lord of creatures named Bharga.
Of Vatsa, Vatsabhumi; of Bharga, Bhargabhumi, born of Bharga. These sons of Angiras were born in the Bhargava line.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, three kinds of sons, in the thousands. Thus these Kashyapas have been told; now hear of Nahusha.
Given by pleased Shakra, Brihadratha obtained it from him; in succession from Brihadratha it passed to King Barhadratha.
Then, Bhima, having killed Jarasandha, gave that excellent chariot with affection to Vasudeva, the delight of the Kauravas.
Yayati, having conquered the earth with its seven continents and oceans, then divided the kingdom among his sons in five parts, the son of Nahusha.
In the eastern direction Yayati placed Yadu, the eldest; in the middle the son of Nahusha consecrated Puru as king.
In the south-east the wise king (placed) Turvasu. By them this whole earth with seven continents and cities
is even today ruled according to region with dharma. Their people I shall tell of later, best of sages.
Having laid aside his bow and arrows, with five bulls among men, the king became old, placing the burden on his kin.
Having put down his weapons, the lord of the earth roamed the earth; King Yayati, unconquered, became content.
Having thus divided the earth, Yayati said to Yadu: "Take my old age, son, for another purpose.
Young in your form, I would roam this earth, placing old age on you." Yadu replied to him:

A request has been promised by me to a Brahmin without specifying; without fulfilling that, king, I shall not take your old age.
brahmapuran:12:27	In old age there are many faults caused by drinking and eating; therefore, king, I do not dare to take your old age.
brahmapuran:12:28	You have many sons dearer than I, king; choose another son to take it, knower of dharma.
Thus addressed by Yadu, the king, filled with anger, the best of speakers, Yayati, censuring his son, said:
What other stage of life is there for you, or what dharma is prescribed, evil-minded, when you disregard me, who am your teacher?
Having thus spoken, Brahmins, in rage he cursed Yadu: "Your people shall be without a kingdom, fool, without doubt."
The king spoke likewise to Druhyu, Turvasu and Anu, best of Brahmins, and when they too refused,
the unconquered Yayati, very angry, cursed them. All has been duly told by me about this, best of Brahmins.
Having thus cursed all four sons older than Puru, the king said the same words to Puru, Brahmins:
Young in your form, I would roam this earth, placing old age on you, Puru, if you agree.
The mighty Puru accepted his father's old age; and Yayati roamed the earth in Puru's form.
Seeking the end of desires, that best of kings, the lord, played with Vishvachi in the Chaitraratha forest.
When the king was satisfied with desires and pleasures, he took back his own old age from Puru.
Here, best of sages, verses were sung by Yayati, by which one should withdraw desires on all sides, like a tortoise its limbs:

Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desires; like fire fed with ghee it only grows more.
brahmapuran:12:41	All the rice and barley on earth, gold, cattle and women are not enough for one man; knowing this, one is not deluded.
brahmapuran:12:42	When one bears no evil feeling toward any being in deed, mind or speech, then one attains Brahman.
brahmapuran:12:43	When one fears none and none fear him, when he neither desires nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
brahmapuran:12:44	The craving that is hard for the dull-witted to abandon, that does not age with one who ages, that is a disease ending in death: for one who gives it up there is happiness.
brahmapuran:12:45	As one ages the hair ages, the teeth age; the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not age even as the body ages.
brahmapuran:12:46	The pleasure of desire in the world and the great divine pleasure do not equal a sixteenth part of the happiness of the extinction of craving.
Having said this, the royal sage entered the forest with his wife and for a long time practised vast austerity.
At the end of his austerity the greatly famed one attained his goal at Bhrigutunga; fasting, he gave up his body and with his wife attained heaven.
In his line, best of sages, there were five best of royal sages, by whom the entire earth was pervaded as by the rays of the sun.
Now I shall tell the lineage of Yadu, honoured by kings; listen: in it Narayana was born, Hari, the upholder of the Vrishni family.
A man who constantly hears this account of Yayati, best of Brahmins, becomes healthy, rich in offspring, long-lived and famous.
named Jayadratha; hence the king was Dridharatha. Dridharatha's son was Vishvajit, Janamejaya.
His heir was Vaikarna; Vikarna was his son. He had a hundred sons, increasers of the family of the Angas.
All these kings born in the Anga lineage have been told by me: truthful, great-souled, rich in offspring, great charioteers.
Best of sages, now listen: I shall tell the lineage of Riceyu, son of Raudrashva, Brahmins.
Riceyu's son was the king Matinara; Matinara had three sons, exceedingly righteous:
Vasurodha, Pratiratha and the righteous Subahu, all knowers of the Vedas, devoted to Brahmins, speakers of truth.
He had a daughter named Ila, best of sages, a Brahman-speaker, a pre-eminent woman; Tamsu approached her.
Tamsu's son was the royal sage Dharmanetra, mighty, a Brahman-speaker, valiant; his wife was Upadanavi.
Then Upadanavi bore four auspicious sons: Dushyanta, Sushmanta, Pravira and the blameless Anagha.
Dushyanta's heir was the valiant Bharata, named Sarvadamana, great, with the strength of ten thousand elephants.
A universal emperor was born as the son of the great-souled Dushyanta on Shakuntala: Bharata, by whose name the Bharatas are called.
When the sons of King Bharata were destroyed through the anger of their mothers, that was told by me before.
The Brahmin great sage Bharadvaja, son of Angiras Brihaspati, the lord, officiated at great sacrifices.
Earlier, when the birth of a son was in vain, then Vitatha was born as a son from Bharadvaja.
When Vitatha was born, Bharata went to heaven; Bharadvaja consecrated Vitatha and went to the forest.
That Vitatha begot five sons: Suhotra, Suhotar, Gaya, Garga,
and the great-souled Kapila; Suhotra's two sons: Kashika and the great truthful king Gritsamati.
Gritsamati's sons were Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas; Kashika's son was Kasheya, and Dirghatapas.
Dirghatapas had a learned son, Dhanvantari; Dhanvantari's son was renowned as Ketuman.
Ketuman's son is remembered as the learned Bhimaratha; Bhimaratha's son became ruler of Varanasi,
famed as Divodasa, destroyer of all Kshatriyas. Divodasa's son was the hero king Pratardana.
Pratardana had two sons, Vatsa and Bhargava; Alarka was a king's son, a king thought well of on earth.
The king took back the Haihaya inheritance, the paternal inheritance Divodasa had taken by force.
By Bhadrashrenya's son, the great-souled Durdama, who was released by Divodasa out of pity as a child,
— a king named Ashtaratha, Bhimaratha's son — by that son the child's (enemy) was struck, Brahmins,
the end of enmity, best of sages, was sought by the Kshatriya. Alarka, king of Kashi, devoted to Brahmins, true to his word,
for sixty thousand years and sixty hundred years was young and endowed with beauty, the upholder of the Kashi family.
By Lopamudra's favour he obtained supreme longevity; at the end of his age, best of sages, having killed the Rakshasa Kshemaka,
the king settled the lovely city of Varanasi. Alarka's heir was the king Kshemaka.
Kshemaka's son was then Varshaketu; Varshaketu's heir was the lord of creatures named Vibhu.
Anarta was Vibhu's son; Sukumara was then born; Sukumara's son was the great charioteer Satyaketu.
His son was the greatly radiant, extremely righteous king; of Vatsa came Vatsabhumi, and of Bhargava, Bhargabhumi.
These sons of Angiras were born in the Bhargava line: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, best of sages.
Hear another lineage, the Ajamidha, best of Brahmins. Suhotra's son was Brihat; Brihat had three sons:
Ajamidha, Dvimidha and the valiant Purumidha. Ajamidha had three renowned wives:
Nili, Keshini and Dhumini, excellent women. On Keshini, Ajamidha begot the mighty Jahnu,
who performed a great session, the Sarvamedha sacrifice, the lord; the Ganga, like a modest woman, desiring him as husband, approached him.
Against his will the Ganga flooded that sacrificial hall; seeing the sacrificial ground flooded all around by her,
Jahnu, the king, angry, Brahmins, said to the Ganga: "In these three worlds I shall gather and drink your waters; Ganga, at once obtain the fruit of this arrogance."
Then, seeing the Ganga drunk, the great-souled great sages brought the fortunate Jahnavi to him as his daughter.
Jahnu married Kaveri, Yuvanashva's daughter, half of whose body was afterwards made a river by the Ganga's curse.
Jahnu's beloved son was the valiant Ajaka; Ajaka's heir was the king Balakashva,
fond of hunting; his son was Kushika, who grew up with Pahlavas and forest-dwellers as a king.
Kushika practised austerity for a son like Indra: "May I obtain one," and Shakra, in fear, came and was born.
He became the king Gadhi, Maghavan Kaushika himself; Vishvamitra was Gadhi's son, and from Vishvamitra, Ashtaka.
Ashtaka's son Lauhi has been named; the Jahnu group was told by me. Hear another lineage, the Ajamidha, best of sages.
From Ajamidha on Nili, Sushanti was born; Sushanti's was Purujati, and from Purujati, Bahyashva.
Bahyashva had five sons, prosperous and ruling countries: Mudgala, Srinjaya, King Brihadishu,
the valiant Yavinara, and Krimilashva the fifth. These five were famed as adequate for protecting the regions.
Of those five came the Panchalas, prosperous and filling countries; they are known as the Panchalas, sufficient for their protection.
Mudgala's heir was the greatly famed Maudgalya, from whom Indrasena got an embryo and a barren (wife).
Panchajana was the son of the great-souled Srinjaya; Panchajana's son was the king Somadatta.
Somadatta's heir was the greatly famed Sahadeva; Sahadeva's son was the renowned Somaka.
Somaka was born as a son of Ajamidha when the line was declining; Somaka's son was Jantu, who had a hundred sons.
The youngest of them was Prishata, father of Drupada, the lord. These are remembered as Ajamidhas, and the great-souled Somakas.
Ajamidha's queen Dhumini, eager for sons, devoted to her husband, fortunate and of good family, best of sages,
desiring a son, goddess, observing vows, practised for ten thousand years supremely difficult austerity.
Having offered into fire by rule, pure, eating moderately, she slept on the kusha grass of the Agnihotra, best of sages.
Ajamidha united with that goddess Dhumini and begot Riksha, smoke-coloured and handsome.
From Riksha was born Samvarana, and from Samvarana, Kuru, who crossed beyond Prayaga and made Kurukshetra,
meritorious and lovely, frequented by the virtuous. His lineage was very great, from whose name the Kauravas come.
Kuru had four sons: Sudhanva, Sudhanus, the mighty-armed Parikshit, and Pravara, conqueror of foes.
Parikshit's heir was the righteous Janamejaya; Shrutasena, Ugrasena and Bhimasena by name —
all these were fortunate, valiant and mighty. Janamejaya's son was the wise Suratha.
Suratha's valiant son Viduratha was born; Viduratha's heir was the great charioteer Riksha.
The second, from Bharadvaja, was famed by that same name: in this Soma line there are two Rikshas and two Parikshits.
